sections.heading: What is Vagal Tone?
sections.content:
Vagal tone refers to the activity level of your vagus nerve - think of it as your nervous system's 'fitness level.' Higher vagal tone means:

• Better ability to calm down after stress
• Easier access to the ventral vagal state
• More emotional regulation capacity
• Stronger connection between mind and body

Like physical fitness, vagal tone can be improved with consistent practice.

sections.heading: Signs of Healthy Vagal Tone
sections.content:
People with good vagal tone tend to experience:

• Quicker recovery from stress
• Better sleep quality
• Easier digestion
• Clearer thinking under pressure
• More stable mood
• Stronger immune function
• Better social connections

You might notice that on 'good days,' several of these come together - that's your vagal tone at work.
sections.practicePrompt: How would you rate your current ability to bounce back from stress? What does recovery look like for you?

sections.heading: Measuring Vagal Tone
sections.content:
Heart Rate Variability (HRV) is the primary way to measure vagal tone. HRV measures the variation in time between heartbeats.

• Higher HRV = Higher vagal tone = More resilience
• Lower HRV = Lower vagal tone = Less flexibility

Many fitness trackers and apps can measure your HRV. It's a useful metric to track over time, though day-to-day fluctuations are normal.
sections.practicePrompt: If you have access to HRV tracking, notice what affects your readings. Sleep, exercise, stress, and connection all play roles.

sections.heading: Building Vagal Tone
sections.content:
You can strengthen vagal tone through consistent practices:

• Slow, deep breathing (especially longer exhales)
• Cold water on face or cold showers
• Singing, humming, or gargling
• Social connection and laughter
• Gentle movement like yoga or tai chi
• Meditation and mindfulness
• Quality sleep

The key is consistency - small daily practices work better than occasional intense efforts.
sections.practicePrompt: Which of these practices appeals to you? Choose one to try this week - even just a few minutes daily can make a difference.

sections.heading: The Breath-Vagus Connection
sections.content:
Your breath is the most direct way to influence your vagus nerve. Here's why:

• When you inhale, your heart rate slightly increases
• When you exhale, your vagus nerve slows your heart
• Longer exhales = More vagal activation = More calm

Try this: Breathe in for 4 counts, out for 6-8 counts. Just a few breaths can start to shift your state.
sections.practicePrompt: Practice the extended exhale breathing right now. Inhale for 4, exhale for 6-8. Do this for 5 breaths and notice how you feel.
